transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Miguel (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood CSM), Liam (CTO - AstraHealth), Sara (Head of ML), Ethan (PM)

Auto-generated Summary: Weekly POC sync focused on benchmark comparisons versus baseline provider CloudServe. Discussed tuning knobs and next steps for canary pilot.

[00:00] Miguel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick roll call, and then Priya will walk through the latest benchmark spreadsheet. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Liam: Good, thanks. We're keen to see the numbers. We've been getting some flak from infra about p99 spikes so hoping you have more detail.
[00:15] Priya: cool, yeah, I pulled the end-to-end numbers - I put the sheet in the shared folder, link in the invite chat, um, and I'll share raw logs after this call.
[00:25] Ethan: link? I think I missed that, can you paste again?
[00:30] Priya: sure - benchmark sheet: https://redwood.app/sheets/ast-poc-bench (note: internal link)

[02:05] Priya: Ok top-line, p50 latency for Redwood hosted was around 60 ms for a 512-token workload, p95 was 190 ms, p99 around 420 ms in our US-west region. CloudServe baseline numbers we measured were p50 75 ms, p95 210 ms, p99 520 ms. Throughput wise we saw about 1.8k tokens/sec per instance on Redwood with adaptive batching vs 1.4k on baseline under the same concurrency.
[02:35] Sara: so overall better but p99 still a bit high - do you have breakdowns whether it's network or model compute?
[02:40] Priya: yes, we instrumented traces - about 60% of p99 is queuing/batching latency during bursts, 25% is model kernel, and ~15% network overhead including TLS handshake for cold connections. We saw significant improvement when we enabled persistent connections / keepalive.

[05:10] Miguel: can you run through the tuning you applied? I remember last week we tried quant 4-bit and different batch windows.
[05:16] Priya: right so for today's run we tried two quant profiles: q4x and q8 at higher perf. q4x gave ~20% token throughput improvement and reduced GPU memory which lets us increase effective batch size, but we also saw a small delta in quality on one of the eval prompts - not dramatic but noted. For batching we used adaptive batching with a 30ms window, then a fallback smaller window on tail latency sensitive route. That reduced average cost by ~12% while keeping p95 within SLA.
[06:03] Liam: what's the SLA threshold again for the pilot? We said p95 under 250ms for E2E.
[06:08] Miguel: yes that's right for pilot acceptance p95 < 250ms and p99 ideally under 500ms but we can roll with mitigations if p99 trips occasionally.

[07:22] Ethan: curious about dedicated vs hosted - for production we might need dedicated, but for the POC we want low friction. What is tradeoff?
[07:30] Priya: Hosted gets you fastest onboarding; dedicated gives predictable throughput and less multi-tenant queuing - we estimate a 10-25% reduction in tail latencies depending on traffic pattern. Also Dedicated lets you pin quantization profiles and model versions. If you need VPC/network isolation that's when Redwood Private comes into play.
[08:10] Sara: we do have some SSO/SSO - SAML - and audit requirements, can you send SOC2 docs?
[08:16] Miguel: Yep, I'll drop the security deck and SOC2 summary after the call. Security deck link: https://redwood.app/security (we'll also attach KMS/HSM notes).

[09:50] Priya: we also compared different instance types - A100-80GB vs older V100-like baseline. Using A100 + our kernel selection gave better utilization; interestingly the baseline provider was on 40GB-equivalent GPUs and we saw more swapping on the baseline runs which spiked p99.
[10:20] Liam: are you sure the baseline was using older hardware? They told us they had A100s in their fleet but perhaps not for our tenancy.
[10:27] Priya: yeah it's tenant-specific; we matched their reported instance type in the baseline column of the sheet but flagged where we were not 1:1. See the 'notes' tab.

[12:00] Miguel: let's surface the real end-to-end numbers - including network from your EU region, cause we expect higher p99 there. Liam, you mentioned infra saw spikes?
[12:08] Liam: yes, when EU users hit a certain concurrency we get tail latency spikes around 700-900 ms for some flows.
[12:15] Priya: that's why we requested region-specific tests. Our last run was US-west - can we get you to execute the small script we sent that simulates your production traffic from EU? It reports p50/p95/p99 and raw traces.
[12:30] Ethan: Sara is running that this week. We'll upload results to the sheet.

[14:40] Priya: quick note on KV cache - enabling prefix caching for repeated context reduced tokens per request by about 18% in our sample workload which also helped reduce cost and tail latency in long-conversation scenarios. If you have many repeated prefixes it's effective.
[15:05] Sara: our chat flow has long context and repeated system prompts, so that could be helpful. Any risk to consistency with caching?
[15:12] Priya: not generally, we have TTLs and validation hooks; but for very dynamic prompts we suggested a conservative cache TTL. We'll document recommended settings in the notebook.

[17:00] Ethan: about quantization quality - you said there was a slight delta for q4x, can we get evals on our in-house prompt set?
[17:08] Priya: yes we ran the eval harness on your sample prompt set (tab 'evals') - q4x had a 0.9% drop on exact match on the retrieval prompts and a minor change in BLEU-like metric; we can run a larger sweep or try hybrid: q8 for sensitive routes, q4x for high-throughput background tasks.
[17:40] Liam: sounds reasonable. For the canary we probably want to route ~10% traffic to q4x variant with canary monitors on latency and quality.

[19:20] Miguel: ok, let's talk about monitoring and rollback thresholds - what metrics should we set?
[19:27] Jordan: recommended: p95 latency > 250ms for 5 min triggers rollback, error rate > 0.5% for 2 min, quality regression more than 2% on eval set for 10 min flags engineer review. We'll share a monitoring playbook.
[19:45] Sara: can you integrate with our PagerDuty?
[19:48] Jordan: yes, we'll include PagerDuty and Datadog hookup steps in the playbook.

[22:05] Priya: on networking - we recommend enabling keepalive and TLS session reuse, plus using our VPC peering if you want lowest e2e latency. For VPC there is some provisioning lead time.
[22:20] Liam: what's lead time for VPC peering / Private deployment?
[22:24] Miguel: typical is 2-3 weeks for VPC peering prep and config, longer for on-prem packaging. We'll scope that once you decide on Dedicated vs Private.

[24:10] Ethan: any surprises in the raw logs?
[24:14] Priya: a few runs had noisy background processes on the baseline instance causing CPU steal, so we marked those runs. Also one test had a transient network routing issue that inflated p99 - raw logs show the spike timestamped, we'll annotate that.

[26:00] Liam: ok, so immediate next actions for us: run EU region script, review notebook, and pick canary percentage.
[26:08] Miguel: we'll provide the recommended canary config and the playbook. Also I'll include pricing options for a 3-month pilot on Dedicated capacity.

[28:33] Sara: curious - any compliance questions around log retention and PII redaction?
[28:40] Jordan: we support configurable retention, redaction hooks, and can integrate with your KMS for at-rest encryption. We'll send the compliance appendix with retention options.

[31:22] Priya: final note: we recommend two follow-up runs - one with q4x enabled for background routes and one with conservative q8 for user-facing. That gives you a direct apples-to-apples.
[31:35] Ethan: cool, let's plan the canary next week then.

[33:00] Miguel: wrap up - thanks everyone. We'll share: 1) full notebook and raw logs (Priya), 2) SOC2/security deck and KMS notes (Miguel), 3) canary playbook and pricing (Miguel/Jordan).
[33:18] Liam: thanks, appreciate it.
[33:20] Sara: thanks all.

[45:00] End of meeting
file_notes: Transcript contains occasional misrecognized product names (e.g., 'Redwood Dedicate' instead of 'Redwood Dedicated') and imperfect timestamps typical of automated transcription. Shared artifacts: benchmark sheet, security deck.
